Because path operations are evaluated in order, you must declare the path for `/users/me` before the one for `/users/{user_id}`. Otherwise, the path for `/users/{user_id}` would also match `/users/me`, "thinking" that it is receiving a parameter `user_id` with a value of `"me"`. [path-params.md]
expected: Path operations are evaluated in order, so otherwise /users/{user_id} would also match /users/me.

To declare a path parameter containing a path, use the `:path` option inside the path declaration:

`/files/{file_path:path}`

In this case, the name of the parameter is `file_path`, and the `:path` syntax tells it to match any path. If you need the path to include a leading slash, use a double slash (e.g., `/files//home/johndoe/myfile.txt`).

[path-params.md]
To return only the fields that were explicitly set, omitting those with default values, you can set the path operation decorator parameter `response_model_exclude_unset=True`. [response-model.md]

To return an HTTP error with a custom status code and message from a path operation, you use `HTTPException`. Because it is a normal Python exception, you `raise` it rather than return it. When you raise an `HTTPException`, you can pass a `detail` parameter (which can be a `str`, `dict`, `list`, etc.) that will be converted to JSON automatically. [handling-errors.md]

If you use the same model for both input and output, you could end up sending a user's password to every client in the API response. 

To avoid this, you can create a separate output model that does not include the password field and declare it in the `response_model` parameter of your path operation. FastAPI will then filter out all data not declared in that output model. [response-model.md]
expected: The password could be returned to clients. Use separate input and output models and set response_model to the output model to filter data.

To run a function after returning a response, you can use `BackgroundTasks`. First, import `BackgroundTasks` and define a parameter in your path operation function with a type declaration of `BackgroundTasks`. FastAPI will create the object and pass it to your function. You then add your task by calling `.add_task()` inside your path operation function, passing the task function and its arguments [background-tasks.md].

Yes, the task function can be an `async def` or a normal `def` function; FastAPI will know how to handle it correctly [background-tasks.md].
expected: Add a BackgroundTasks parameter and call add_task(function, args). The function can be def or async def.
